classification.difficultyReason: Use the explicitly prompted longest-side fact to justify sine and cosine bounds, then recognise that tangent can exceed one because either perpendicular side can be longer.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Which is the largest side of a right-angled triangle?

answer.worked: The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle, the largest angle, so it is the longest side.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Is it possible for values of $\sin\theta$ to be greater than 1? Why?

answer.short: No. The opposite side is shorter than the hypotenuse.
answer.worked: $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$. The numerator is smaller than the denominator, so $0<\sin\theta<1$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Is it possible for values of $\cos\theta$ to be greater than 1? Why?

answer.short: No. The adjacent side is shorter than the hypotenuse.
answer.worked: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$. The numerator is smaller than the denominator, so $0<\cos\theta<1$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Is it possible for values of $\tan\theta$ to be greater than 1? Why?

answer.short: Yes. The opposite side can be longer than the adjacent side.
answer.worked: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$. When the opposite side is longer than the adjacent side, this ratio is greater than 1.
